subtype: Approach: picks a partner who excuses everything [Pitfall]
passage: With two weeks before the final exam, Aditi asked her close friend Siddharth to be her check-in partner. "Every night, ask whether I did my hours," she said. Night one, she had done two hours of four. "It's fine," said Siddharth. "You've been working hard. Take a break." Night two, one hour. "Honestly, me too. Let's watch one episode." By night six the check-ins were texts like "ugh, same" and "tomorrow?" Nobody pushed. The pile of unfinished chapters stayed exactly the same size. On night twelve Aditi looked at the calendar and saw two days left. She felt sick. She had told herself that the partner was helping, and all they had really shared was excuses.

qa.q: How many hours of the four had Aditi done on the first night?
qa.a: Aditi had done two hours of four on night one.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel on night twelve?
qa.a: Aditi felt sick with worry and regret at how little had changed.

qa.q: What could Aditi look for in a partner instead?
qa.a: Aditi could look for a partner who asks honestly about the plan and gently says when a target was missed, or add a written goal.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have meant "Take a break"?
qa.a: Siddharth probably meant it kindly, wanting Aditi to rest, without seeing that it hurt her plan.

grounding: Shows a student choosing a partner who excuses everything so the check-ins become shared excuses and nothing changes.
